summary.text: A river mouth is the place where a river flows into a larger body of water, such as another river, a lake, a bay, a sea or an ocean.
There the current slows and can carry less, so the river drops sediment that builds landforms such as deltas, sand bars and spits.
These landforms reshape the coast and its wildlife, and sand bars shelter sensitive ecosystems enriched by nutrients the river brings.

facts.label: Landforms built
facts.value: Deltas, sand bars, spits and tie channels

facts.label: Fresh water entering sea
facts.value: Usually floats along the surface as an overflow

facts.label: English place names
facts.value: Plymouth: the mouth of the Plym River

facts.label: Celtic place names
facts.value: Aber or Inver, as in Aberdeen and Inverness

facts.label: Effect of dams
facts.value: Starve the mouth of sand and nutrients

items.prompt: Fresh river water pours out into the salty sea. What does the river water typically do as it enters?

options.label: Sinks straight to the seabed
Mixes evenly top to bottom at once
Spreads out along the surface
Turns back upstream with the waves

items.explain: Fresh river water is usually lighter than seawater, so it floats along the surface as an overflow.

items.prompt: Why does a river tend to drop the sand and silt it is carrying when it reaches its mouth?

options.label: Salt in the sea makes sand grains heavier
Its current slows, so it can carry less
The water gets colder and freezes the mud
Fish and plants filter the sand out

items.explain: At the mouth the current slows, which reduces how much sediment the water can carry, so the sediment is deposited.

items.prompt: A large dam is built far upstream on a river. What tends to happen at the river's mouth over the following years?

options.label: It gets far more sand and nutrients than before
Its sand bars grow taller from trapped water
Its water becomes saltier than the open sea
It runs short of the sand and nutrients it needs

items.explain: Damming can starve the river of sand and nutrients, leaving a deficit at its mouth.

items.prompt: Many towns and cities around the world were founded right where a river meets the sea. What is one reason?

options.label: They offer easy travel and good sites for ports
They are the places least likely to ever flood
They have the coldest and steadiest weather
They are always the highest ground nearby

items.explain: River mouths allow easy travel and ports and are sites of large-scale sediment deposition, so many towns and cities grew there.

items.prompt: In Celtic-derived place names such as Aberdeen and Inverness, what do the starting parts 'Aber' and 'Inver' refer to?

options.label: A high hill or mountain
A castle or fort
A thick forest
A river's mouth

items.explain: Aber and Inver are the Celtic terms for a river mouth, just as '-mouth' is in English names like Plymouth.

items.prompt: A sand bar builds up across the coast at a river's mouth. How does this tend to affect the life in the waters behind it?

options.label: It cuts off all nutrients, so life dies off
It shelters it, while the river brings nutrients
It floods it with salt water at every tide
It has no effect, since bars are underwater

items.explain: Along coasts, sand bars act as barriers that shelter sensitive ecosystems enriched by nutrients the river deposits.
